target.title: Direct classification of all American English phonemes using signals from functional speech motor cortex
target.version: Author manuscript; published in final edited form 2014 May 19

read.pdf: Figs. 1–6 captions read in text.txt; no tables; PDF itself not supplied

entries.text: The study directly classifies the full General American English phoneme inventory from ECoG signals recorded over functional speech motor cortex.
entries.condition: Spoken/read words; phonemes are the classification targets; ECoG acquired during clinical extraoperative monitoring.
entries.quote: In this study, we investigated words that span the entire set of phonemes in the General American accent using ECoG with 4 subjects.

entries.text: The authors claim this is the first ECoG study to decode the entire American English phoneme set and the first to classify individual phonemes within word production.
entries.condition: The authors' novelty claim is scoped to ECoG phoneme decoding and the General American English inventory.
entries.quote: This study is the first to decode the entire set of phonemes from American English using ECoG.

entries.text: They state that, to their knowledge, earlier ECoG studies had not treated phonemes as independent events within words, aligned with millisecond precision, or classified a comprehensive language-wide phoneme set.
entries.condition: Prior-work scope as described by the authors in the introduction.

entries.text: The cohort comprised four participants, mean age 42 years, two female; all required extraoperative ECoG monitoring for intractable seizures.
entries.unit: subjects; years mean age; female subjects
entries.condition: Clinical patients recruited during extraoperative seizure monitoring; electrode coverage was determined by medical necessity.
entries.quote: Four subjects (mean age 42, 2 female) who required extraoperative ECoG monitoring for treatment of their intractable seizures gave informed consent to participate in this study.

entries.text: ECoG sampling rates were 500 Hz for NU1, 1 kHz for NU2/NU3, and 9.6 kHz for MC1.
entries.condition: Clinical acquisition settings varied by subject: NU1 500 Hz; NU2 and NU3 1 kHz; MC1 9.6 kHz.

entries.text: Speech audio was recorded at 44.1 kHz using a USB microphone and synchronized with ECoG.
entries.condition: Simultaneous microphone and ECoG recordings; microphone audio was used to identify phoneme onsets.

entries.text: ECoG was bandpass filtered at 0.5–300 Hz for NU2, NU3, MC1 and 0.5–120 Hz for NU1.
entries.condition: Filtering was subject-specific: NU2/NU3/MC1 0.5–300 Hz; NU1 0.5–120 Hz.

entries.text: Participants read each prompted word aloud; each word appeared for 3 seconds followed by a 1-second blank.
entries.unit: seconds per word display; seconds blank interval
entries.condition: Visually presented word-reading task using BCI2000; subjects were encouraged to begin speaking as soon as the word appeared.

entries.text: The stimulus inventory combined the 300-word Modified Rhyme Test with 20 added words to include four phonemes missing from the MRT.
entries.unit: MRT words; additional words; additional phonemes
entries.condition: The resulting word set was intended to cover the General American English phoneme inventory; words were read aloud.

entries.text: NU1 and MC1 each completed 320 word trials; NU2 and NU3 completed 480, with the first 160 stimulus words repeated.
entries.condition: Per-subject total trial count depended on clinical availability; the 480-word sessions included a repeat of the first 160 stimulus words.
entries.quote: Total trials per subject varied from 320 words (Subjects NU1 and MC1) to 480 words

entries.text: Each participant contributed at least 600 consonant and 320 vowel phonemes.
entries.unit: minimum consonant phonemes; minimum vowel phonemes per subject
entries.condition: Across the 320- or 480-word task, per-subject minimum counts; exact counts varied with the completed word trials.

entries.text: The analyzed data included 981 phonemes for the 320-word set and 1,470 for the 480-word set; 67.3% were consonants.
entries.condition: Reported for full stimulus sets at the two trial-count levels; 1,470 applies to subjects completing 480 words.

entries.text: Phoneme identities were assigned with the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary; onset times were manually labeled from visual and auditory microphone-signal changes.
entries.condition: Dictionary assumes General American pronunciation; human annotators marked each phoneme onset from recorded speech audio.
entries.quote: We inspected visual and auditory spectral changes in the microphone signal to manually label the onset of each phoneme within each word.

entries.text: ECoG was common-average referenced; spectral power was expressed relative to baseline activity in the first second of each 4-second trial.
entries.unit: seconds per trial; second baseline interval
entries.condition: Trials centered on word onset; common-average reference in the time domain and baseline-relative power computation.

entries.text: Features used short-time Fourier transforms on 150-ms moving windows, 2-Hz frequency steps, and 50-ms shifts spanning 300 ms before to 300 ms after phoneme onset (12 bins).
entries.unit: ms windows; Hz frequency step; ms shifts; ms each side of onset; time bins
entries.condition: ECoG electrode features were created for each phoneme; the 12 bins included the phoneme and preparatory activity.
entries.quote: We computed features by shifting the 150-ms window in 50-ms increments, and used the features from 300 ms prior to 300 ms after phoneme onset.

entries.text: The feature set comprised three high-gamma sub-bands (65–115, 125–175, 185–250 Hz), mu (7–13 Hz), beta (15–30 Hz), and local motor potential.
entries.condition: Power features per electrode and time bin; local motor potential was the time-domain signal smoothed over 150 ms.

entries.text: Features were ranked by one-way ANOVA p-values across phonemes during training, then the 140 lowest-p-value features were selected for LDA.
entries.condition: Feature selection performed using training data; features were derived from electrode, frequency-band, and time-bin combinations.

entries.text: The feature count was tuned by increasing it until performance peaked; LDA was chosen primarily for feature interpretability.
entries.condition: No separate validation procedure is described for feature-count selection; see t66.
entries.quote: The optimal number of features was determined by systematically increasing the value until decoding performance reached a maximum.

entries.text: The phoneme decoder was linear discriminant analysis (LDA), a closed-set classifier over the phoneme classes.
entries.condition: Offline classification of phoneme labels from the selected ECoG features; no word-level decoder training is reported.
entries.quote: The 140 features with the lowest p-values were selected to classify phonemes using linear discriminant analysis (LDA) [ 25 ], [ 28 ].

entries.text: Success rates were estimated using 10-fold cross-validation with randomly selected test folds, reported as independent of each other and the training sets.
entries.condition: Cross-validation conducted for each subject; random trial-level test sets; no separate subject-held-out test is reported.
entries.quote: We used 10-fold cross-validation with randomly-selected test sets, which were fully independent of each other and of the training sets, to compute success rates.

entries.text: Reported decoding percentages average five separate repetitions of 10-fold cross-validation, or 50 folds total.
entries.condition: Repeated cross-validation was used to reduce sensitivity to phoneme distribution within folds.

entries.text: Chance classification was estimated by randomly shuffling phoneme labels and rerunning classification 100 times.
entries.condition: The paper does not specify whether shuffles were stratified by class, subject, or fold; see t68.

entries.text: For peak subject performance, electrodes without significant features (p > 0.1) or significant activity before/during onset were excluded; the remaining set was used to select 140 features.
entries.unit: p-value threshold; selected features; minimum possible candidate features
entries.condition: Subject-specific electrode exclusion for peak-performance analysis; at least four electrodes, 12 bins, and five bands plus LMP supplied at least 288 candidate features.
entries.quote: This prevented electrodes associated with auditory areas from confounding motor speech decoding.

entries.text: Across the four subjects, all-phoneme accuracy averaged 20.4 ± 9.8%, above the shuffled chance level of 7.4% (p < 0.001, t-test).
entries.unit: % accuracy mean ± SD; % chance; t-test p-value
entries.condition: All phonemes; average across four subjects; 50-fold cross-validation repetitions; chance estimated from shuffled labels.
entries.quote: Averaged across all subjects, 20.4±9.8% of all phonemes were classified correctly, significantly greater than chance decoding (7.4%, p<0.001, t-test).

entries.text: The authors report up to 36% accuracy when classifying all phonemes.
entries.condition: Best subject-specific performance for the full phoneme classification task; the abstract does not name the subject, while the results identify NU2 as highest-performing.
entries.quote: We classified phonemes with up to 36% accuracy when classifying all phonemes and up to 63% accuracy for a single phoneme.

entries.text: Best single-phoneme accuracy was 63% for /k/ in subject NU2.
entries.condition: One phoneme class /k/; NU2; 50-fold cross-validation average; peak-performance electrode-selection procedure.

entries.text: Vowel classification averaged 19.2 ± 3.7%, compared with a 12.9% shuffled chance level (p < 0.01, t-test).
entries.unit: % accuracy mean ± SD; % chance; t-test p-value
entries.condition: Vowels across all four subjects; cross-validated; chance estimated by label shuffling.
entries.quote: Average classification performance for vowels across all subjects was 19.2±3.7%, also significantly greater than chance (12.9%, p<0.01, t-test), with the best performance in NU2 of 23.9%.

entries.text: The best vowel accuracy was 23.9% in NU2.
entries.condition: Vowels only; NU2; subject-specific cross-validation.
entries.quote: with the best performance in NU2 of 23.9%.

entries.text: NU2 had the highest overall performance, correctly classifying 36.1% of consonant phonemes.
entries.condition: Consonant phonemes; NU2; best-performing subject; cross-validated result.
entries.quote: Subject NU2 had the highest overall performance, in which 36.1% of consonant phonemes were correctly classified.

entries.text: Misclassified phonemes were 15.5% more likely to be assigned to a direct IPA neighbor than a distant phoneme; for NU2 the difference was 24.2%.
entries.condition: Misclassification incidence compared for direct IPA neighbors versus phonemes distant on the IPA chart; overall and NU2-specific comparison.

entries.text: Misclassifications were 34.3% more likely to involve a phoneme with a similar vocal-tract constriction location, rising to 49.8% for NU2.
entries.condition: Comparison of phoneme confusions by vocal-tract constriction location; all-subject result and NU2-specific result.

entries.text: The authors note that the poorest-performing phonemes had fewer than 10 repetitions.
entries.condition: Low-frequency phoneme classes; number of trials below 10 was associated with poorest classification.

entries.text: Restricting NU2 classification to the four most frequent phonemes yielded a maximum accuracy of 72.3%.
entries.condition: Subset classification for NU2, using the four most frequent phonemes in the data; not full-inventory accuracy.
entries.quote: This process yields a maximum performance of 72.3% using 4 phonemes for Subject NU2 ( Figure 5a ).

entries.text: Adding Gaussian onset-time noise with a 100-ms standard deviation sharply reduced classification performance.
entries.unit: ms standard deviation of onset-time noise
entries.condition: Onset alignment sensitivity analysis; noise added to manually identified phoneme onset times.
entries.quote: This result demonstrates the critical need for temporal precision in phonemic analysis, as performance sharply decreases as timing offset noise increases.

entries.text: Mean phoneme duration was 176 ms, with a reported range from 75 ms for /b/ to 282 ms for /s/.
entries.unit: ms mean; ms minimum example; ms maximum example
entries.condition: Durations in the spoken-word task; cited to contextualize the 100-ms onset-noise result.
entries.quote: which is notably less than the 176 ms average length of a phoneme in time (ranging from 75 ms for \b\ to 282 ms for \s\).

entries.text: The 65–115-Hz high-gamma band reached a mean 79.8% of each subject's maximum decoding value.
entries.condition: Single-band decoding using all electrodes; mean across subjects; band 65–115 Hz.
entries.quote: mean of 79.8% of maximum decoding values across subjects for the 65-115 Hz band

entries.text: Mu-band decoding reached 50.7% of maximum decoding values and was significantly above chance (p < 0.05).
entries.condition: Mu-band single-band decoding; averaged across subjects as reported.
entries.quote: The mu band also showed significantly better than chance decoding (50.7% of maximum decoding values, p < 0.05).

entries.text: The local motor potential and beta bands did not decode phonemes significantly better than chance (p > 0.1).
entries.condition: Individual-band decoding analysis; local motor potential and beta bands.
entries.quote: Local motor potential and beta bands could not decode phonemes significantly better than chance performance (p > 0.1).

entries.text: The most informative time bin was 0–50 ms after onset; features from 200 ms before through 200 ms after onset accounted for 88.1% of peak performance.
entries.unit: ms onset bin; ms either side; % of peak performance
entries.condition: Time-bin analysis across subjects; the 200-ms pre/post interval spans causal preparation and early phoneme production.
entries.quote: When combined, features spanning 200 ms before to 200 ms after phoneme onset accounted for 88.1% of peak performance.

entries.text: Each subject had at least four electrodes with causal information useful for decoding speech articulation.
entries.condition: Electrodes contained causal speech-related information; information was concentrated in functional facial motor areas.

entries.text: The authors report that most phoneme information came from functional facial motor areas and that high-gamma features were most informative.
entries.condition: Results are based on clinically placed ECoG electrodes; coverage varied by subject.

entries.text: For NU2, 14.8% of consonant combinations in the stimulus set were identified without training the algorithm to decode words; chance was 0.83% (p < 0.0001, t-test).
entries.condition: Consonant combinations in the 320-word stimulus set; NU2; phoneme classifier was not trained on words.

entries.text: Restricting whole-word predictions to words in the stimulus set raised word identification from 14.8% to 18.8%.
entries.condition: NU2 phoneme predictions; constrained to the words in the study stimulus set, ordered by posterior probability; no word-level decoder was trained.

entries.text: The authors estimate a hypothetical BCI information transfer rate of 3.0 bits/s, equivalent to 33.6 words/min.
entries.condition: Derived from word/phoneme identification and speech duration assumptions; hypothetical, not a live BCI measurement; word predictions constrained to the stimulus vocabulary for the 18.8% result.
entries.quote: We calculated an information transfer rate of 3.0 bits/sec (equivalent to 33.6 words per minute) for a hypothetical BCI ( Figure 6 ).

entries.text: The ITR calculation used mean word duration 520 ms and mean phoneme duration 176 ms.
entries.unit: ms mean word duration; ms mean phoneme duration
entries.condition: Measured in this spoken-word task; information capacity per phoneme was multiplied by classification success and speech rate.

entries.text: The authors stress that word identification is not strict word decoding because phoneme onsets were supplied in advance.
entries.condition: Analysis uses known phoneme onset locations; it does not detect attempted speech onset or decode unconstrained continuous speech.

entries.text: The authors state that 18.8% word identification is insufficient for communication, despite demonstrating word identification from phoneme analysis.
entries.condition: Stimulus-set-constrained word predictions; NU2; not an end-to-end online communication result.

entries.text: A theoretical volitional-control channel for /k/ in NU2 was estimated to yield 32 words/min.
entries.condition: Theoretical single-/k/-channel calculation for NU2; computed similarly to cited comparison ITRs, not measured online word output.

entries.text: The introduction cites 2.1 bits/s as the information rate of the then-most-efficient communication BCI.
entries.condition: Prior BCI benchmark cited in the introduction; this is not a measurement from the target study.
entries.quote: information rates of 2.1 bits/s

entries.text: A prior intracortical-spike study was reported to classify all phonemes with up to 21% success.
entries.condition: Prior chronic intracortical microelectrode study; classification of the full phoneme set as described in the target paper.
entries.quote: Speech BCIs using intracortically-recorded spikes to decode phonemes have achieved up to 21% classification success of all phonemes

entries.text: A prior study reported up to 70% discrimination of three imagined vowels in one participant with locked-in syndrome.
entries.condition: Imagined-vowel task in an individual with locked-in syndrome; prior intracortical BMI work.

entries.text: An earlier ECoG study classified a restricted subset of four phonemes.
entries.condition: Prior ECoG subset-classification study; the target paper also cites a separate two-phoneme study.

entries.text: The authors say phoneme confusions follow articulatory/IPA organization, supporting the claim that cortical activity contains phonetic structure.
entries.condition: Error analysis compares confusion patterns to IPA place and manner organization; it is descriptive evidence, not an independent decoding benchmark.

entries.text: The authors recommend a high-density 1–2-mm electrode array over at least 4 cm of speech motor cortex as a promising future configuration.
entries.unit: mm electrode spacing; cm cortical coverage
entries.condition: Future design recommendation based on target-study spatial findings and prior work; not tested in this four-subject study.

entries.text: Electrode coverage varied widely because placement was clinically determined, which the authors identify as a major source of between-subject performance variation.
entries.condition: Four epilepsy patients; electrode coverage determined by clinical need, not standardized experimental placement.

entries.text: The authors warn that the temporal precision required by this method poses challenges for real-time translation to locked-in patients and may require a separate attempted-speech onset detector.
entries.condition: Offline phoneme analysis relies on precisely identified phoneme events; no onset-detection solution was evaluated.

entries.text: The authors say repetition counts were limited by clinical constraints, although they expect more phoneme repetitions to improve classification.
entries.condition: Clinical patient availability limited repeated examples; no additional-data experiment was reported.

entries.text: The authors caution that comparisons with other ECoG speech studies are difficult because phoneme sets, trial counts, decoding methods, and electrode coverage differ substantially.
entries.condition: Cross-study comparison; target paper estimates ITR to permit approximate comparison.

entries.text: The evaluation does not report a held-out-subject/speaker test; reported cross-validation is within individual subjects, so speaker-independent generalization is not established.
entries.condition: The methods describe random 10-fold test sets and results are subject-specific; no training-on-some-speakers/testing-on-unseen-speakers protocol is stated.
entries.quote: We used 10-fold cross-validation with randomly-selected test sets, which were fully independent of each other and of the training sets, to compute success rates.

entries.text: No session-held-out evaluation or recording-session boundaries are reported; performance across separate days/sessions is unknown.
entries.condition: Random test-fold protocol is described, but session identifiers, session counts, and session-disjoint partitions are not given.
entries.quote: We used 10-fold cross-validation with randomly-selected test sets, which were fully independent of each other and of the training sets, to compute success rates.

entries.text: Randomization seeds are not reported for cross-validation folds, repeated runs, or label shuffles.
entries.condition: Five repetitions and 100 chance shuffles are specified, but seed values or deterministic randomization settings are absent.

entries.text: The paper does not specify nested cross-validation or an independent validation set for choosing feature count, individual time bins/bands, or peak-performance electrodes; selection-related optimism cannot be assessed.
entries.condition: ANOVA ranking is stated to use training data, but the data used to tune the number of features and other analysis choices is not fully described.
entries.quote: The optimal number of features was determined by systematically increasing the value until decoding performance reached a maximum.

entries.text: Feature-wise scaling/standardization before LDA is not specified; the paper reports common-average referencing and baseline-relative spectral power only.
entries.condition: Preprocessing reports time-domain common-average referencing and power relative to the first second, but no additional feature normalization method.

entries.text: The paper does not state whether phoneme-label shuffling preserved class frequencies or was performed within each subject/fold, nor whether feature/model selection was repeated for each shuffle.
entries.condition: Chance is described as random label shuffling followed by reclassification for 100 repetitions; further shuffle protocol details are omitted.

entries.text: The article does not say whether cross-validation folds were grouped by word; lexical items or repeated presentations may therefore occur across training and test folds.
entries.condition: Words were repeated for NU2/NU3 and test folds were randomly selected; a word-disjoint or repetition-grouped split is not described.
entries.quote: We used 10-fold cross-validation with randomly-selected test sets, which were fully independent of each other and of the training sets, to compute success rates.

entries.text: No trained language model or unconstrained-vocabulary word decoder is reported; the word-identification analysis optionally restricts predictions to the study's stimulus words.
entries.condition: Phoneme LDA outputs are combined for word identification; the constrained condition uses only stimulus-set words, and the authors describe speech-recognition algorithms as future work.

entries.text: The report does not give a session- or participant-specific prospective test condition or a prospective real-time evaluation; ITR is an estimate for a hypothetical BCI.
entries.condition: Classification is cross-validated offline; ITR is calculated analytically from durations and phoneme/word success rather than measured in online use.

entries.text: The sample-size analysis classified all 24 consonant phonemes using increasing numbers of samples.
entries.condition: Analysis of accuracy versus phoneme sample count; all consonant classes were included.

entries.text: For all subjects, performance declined as phoneme classes were added until approximately 15 classes; additional rarer phonemes had fewer than 10 samples.
entries.condition: Classification accuracy versus number of included phonemes; additional classes were less frequent in the data.

entries.text: The introduction cites 25 bits/s as the average natural efficiency of human speech production.
entries.condition: Prior information-transfer-rate estimate cited in the introduction; not measured by the target study.

entries.text: The target text explicitly identifies 24 consonant phoneme classes.
entries.condition: class-count analysis
entries.quote: we classified all 24 consonant phonemes using increasing number of samples

entries.text: The vowel-class count and combined total class count are not stated in the supplied target text.
entries.condition: all-phoneme classification

entries.text: Phoneme onsets were manually labelled from microphone speech.
entries.condition: within each word

entries.text: Yes; feature windows were defined relative to phoneme onset, including for analyzed test events.
entries.condition: features span 300 ms before to 300 ms after phoneme onset

entries.text: Held-out trials were randomly selected and independent of training sets.
entries.condition: success-rate estimation

entries.text: The paper describes electrode exclusion for peak performance but does not say whether that selection was repeated within training folds or performed on all data.
entries.condition: peak-performance analysis
entries.quote: To determine peak performance for each subject, we excluded electrodes that did not contain significant features (p-values > 0.1) or that had no significant activity changes prior to or during phoneme onset.

entries.condition: naive Bayes; 39 phonemes; 1 s of neural population activity per trial

entries.condition: phoneme matrices

entries.value: fold count and partition scheme unstated

entries.text: The closed stimulus set contained 36 English monosyllabic CVC words built from four vowels and nine consonant pairs; these were real words, not pseudowords.
entries.condition: Vowels /ε/, /æ/, /i:/, /u:/; consonant pairs /b_t/, /c_n/, /h_d/, /l_d/, /m_n/, /p_p/, /r_d/, /s_t/, /t_n/.
entries.quote: This structure allowed us to group the words based on either the vowel within the word (_V_) or the leading/trailing consonant pair (C_C).

entries.text: The authors used 25% chance accuracy for four-class vowel and matched four-class consonant-pair classification.
entries.condition: Four categories in each matched-group classifier; consonant groups sampled from nine possible pairs.
entries.quote: all of which were above chance level (i.e., 25% for four-vowel matched groups classification and for nine-consonant-pair matched groups classification).

entries.text: Mean vowel accuracy at the best location was 40.7±2.7% for overt and 37.5±5.9% for covert speech.
entries.condition: Across subjects; overt n=8 and covert n=6; individual-location performance; four-vowel classification with ten-fold CV.

entries.text: Mean consonant-pair accuracy at the best location was 40.6±8.3% for overt and 36.3±9.7% for covert speech.
entries.condition: Across subjects; overt n=8 and covert n=6; best location; four matched consonant-pair classes averaged across all combinations.

entries.text: The authors claim this is the first demonstration of vowel and consonant decoding from spoken or imagined monosyllabic words using human ECoG, alongside cortical localization.
entries.value: first demonstration, as claimed by authors
entries.condition: Vowels and consonants embedded in spoken or imagined monosyllabic words; human ECoG.

entries.text: [later] Audio-derived onset biases inflate overt-speech decoding modestly: realignment reduced first-phoneme accuracy by 12.9%.
entries.condition: First phoneme of each word; neural realignment vs voice-onset labels.
entries.quote: Because we observed an appreciable difference between decoder performance with and without this neural realignment (a 12.9% reduction in accuracy when classifying the first phoneme of each word), we caution that future speech BCI work based on voice onset labels should explicitly take across-labels timing biases into account.

entries.text: [later] Wilson concludes that audio-derived onset biases inflate overt decoding accuracy only modestly.
entries.condition: Overt speech.
entries.quote: This indicates that that audio-derived phoneme onset biases inflate overt speech decoding accuracies, but only modestly so.

entries.text: [later] Removing acoustic contamination by LRR lowered all-phoneme accuracy from 29.3% to 25.8%.
entries.condition: 39 phonemes; linear decoder; after LRR re-referencing.
entries.quote: there was only a small reduction in cross-validated accuracy decoding all phonemes (reduction from 29.3% to 25.8%, Fig. 5D)

entries.text: [later] Wilson finds microphonic artifacts in intracortical and ECoG recordings during overt speech.
entries.condition: Overt speech.
entries.quote: In summary, our results support the concern raised by that microphonic artifacts are present in intracortical and ECoG recordings during overt speech.

entries.text: [later] Sentence decoding reached 9.1% WER on a 50-word and 23.8% WER on a 125,000-word vocabulary.
entries.condition: Attempted speech, one participant, intracortical.
entries.quote: achieved a 9.1% word error rate on a 50-word vocabulary (2.7 times fewer errors than the previous state-of-the-art speech BCI) and a 23.8% word error rate on a 125,000-word vocabulary

entries.text: [later] An RNN trained with connectionist temporal classification emits phoneme probabilities over time, so no phoneme onsets are given at test.
entries.condition: Sentence decoding.
entries.quote: Second, an RNN converts a time series of this neural activity into a time series of probabilities for each phoneme (plus the probability of an interword ‘silence’ token and a ‘blank’ token associated with the connectionist temporal classification training procedure).

entries.text: Bouchard et al. classify cortical locations by articulator with k-nearest neighbours (a map, not a speech-unit classifier).
entries.condition: ECoG, CV syllables.
entries.quote: We then used a k-nearest neighbor algorithm to classify the surrounding cortical tissue based on the nearest k = 4 neighbors within a spatial extent of 3 mm of each spatial location; if no data points were present within 3 mm, the location is unclassified (white).

entries.text: Tankus et al. recorded depth-electrode units while patients uttered one of five vowels.
entries.condition: 11 patients; isolated vowels or CV syllables.
entries.quote: Following an auditory cue, subjects uttered one of five vowels

entries.text: Chen et al. measure PCC between decoded and ground-truth spectrograms (speech reconstruction).
entries.condition: Reconstruction metric.

entries.text: [later] Phoneme prediction was above chance in both Wilson participants.
entries.condition: T5 and T11

questions.q: What exactly is classified, and how broad is the evaluated vocabulary?
questions.answer: The primary decoder classifies phonemes from prompted spoken words, using the full General American inventory assembled from the 300-word MRT plus 20 added words. The downstream word-identification result is restricted to the study stimulus vocabulary in its 18.8% condition.

questions.q: What is the strongest full-inventory result, and what are its evaluation conditions?
questions.answer: The paper reports up to 36% full-inventory accuracy; across four subjects, mean all-phoneme accuracy was 20.4 ± 9.8% versus 7.4% shuffled chance. Evaluation used subject-specific 10-fold cross-validation averaged over five repetitions.

questions.q: Does the study demonstrate an operational real-time speech BCI?
questions.answer: No. Phoneme onsets were manually identified, results were cross-validated offline, word identification used known phoneme onsets and optionally a closed stimulus lexicon, and the 3.0 bits/s rate is explicitly hypothetical.

questions.q: What generalization limits should a review state?
questions.answer: The report does not establish held-out-speaker, held-out-session, or word-disjoint generalization; it also omits random seeds and full details of feature-selection validation, normalization, and the label-shuffle chance procedure.

questions.q: Which limitations do the authors themselves acknowledge?
questions.answer: Performance varied with clinical electrode coverage and limited repetitions; precise event timing complicates real-time translation; the reported word-identification rate is not enough for communication; and cross-study comparisons are difficult.

questions.q: Class counts in the all-phoneme analysis; whether test windows sit on manually labelled onsets; whether peak-performance electrode selection was nested in folds; comparator conditions for Wilson 2020, Willett 2023 and Brumberg 2011.
questions.answer: 24 consonant classes stated; vowel and total class counts not stated, vowels and consonants analysed separately (q1, q1b). Features are taken around manually labelled onsets for every analysed phoneme (q2a, q2b). Electrode exclusion nesting unstated (q3). Wilson 2020: 39 phonemes in spoken words, manual Praat onsets, 33.9% RNN, chance 6% (w1-w4). Willett 2023: 39 isolated attempted phonemes, 62% naive Bayes (k1a, k1b). Brumberg 2011: attempted isolated phonemes, 38 classes, 16-21%, chance 2.6%, ten-fold CV (b1a-b2d).

questions.q: Triage of the evaluation (2026-11-26): second first claim, peak configuration, neighbouring phonemes, 12 bins, Wilson matched comparison and confounds, Willett sequence decoding, Bouchard and Tankus.
questions.answer: Answered by targeted reads of the passages; entries q4-q8, w5-w10, k3-k4, bo1, tk1, ch2.
